subtopics.title: inference
subtopics.teaching: Infer meaning from explicit textual evidence plus reasonable implications. Distinguish what a passage states from what it strongly suggests, and use surrounding details to constrain interpretation.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: If a character repeatedly checks the empty station clock and watches the road, infer that the character is waiting for someone rather than merely describing the setting.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not select an inference that is merely possible; the best answer must be supported by multiple clues and should not contradict the passage.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: make evidence-based inferences, cite the clues that support them, reject unsupported interpretations, and distinguish inference from fact.

subtopics.title: author purpose
subtopics.teaching: Identify why an author chose to write a passage: to inform, explain, persuade, entertain, compare, criticize, reflect, or achieve another specific communicative goal. Use the whole passage rather than one sentence.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: A passage presents statistics, addresses a common objection, and ends with a recommendation; its primary purpose is likely persuasion supported by evidence.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not confuse topic with purpose. A passage about recycling is not necessarily written merely 'about recycling'; its purpose may be to persuade readers to change behaviour.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify primary and secondary purposes, connect purpose to textual choices, and reject answers that describe only the topic.

subtopics.title: tone
subtopics.teaching: Identify tone from diction, imagery, syntax, attitude, and context. Distinguish the author's attitude toward the subject from the emotional reaction a reader might have.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: Words such as 'remarkable,' 'carefully designed,' and 'promising' create an approving or optimistic tone rather than a neutral one.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not label tone from a single emotionally charged word; consider whether the passage as a whole is formal, skeptical, admiring, humorous, critical, urgent, or restrained.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: justify tone with precise language evidence, distinguish closely related tones, and explain how wording creates the identified attitude.

subtopics.title: argument structure
subtopics.teaching: Trace an argument through claim, reasons, evidence, assumptions, counterclaims, and conclusion. Determine how each part contributes to the writer's overall position.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: A writer claims school gardens improve learning, supports the claim with two studies, answers a cost objection, and concludes with a recommendation; those moves form a structured argument.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not treat every statement as a main claim. Examples and statistics may support a claim without being the argument's central position.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: map an argument, identify supporting and opposing components, evaluate logical connections, and explain how structure strengthens or weakens the case.

subtopics.title: evidence evaluation
subtopics.teaching: Evaluate whether evidence is relevant, sufficient, credible, representative, and correctly connected to a claim. Distinguish direct evidence from anecdote, assumption, and opinion.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: One student's experience may illustrate a possibility but cannot by itself establish that an educational policy works for all students.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not equate a precise number with strong evidence. Data can still be irrelevant, biased, outdated, or interpreted beyond what it supports.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: match evidence to claims, identify weaknesses in support, recognize overgeneralization, and select the strongest evidence for a conclusion.

subtopics.title: roots
subtopics.teaching: Use common Greek and Latin roots to infer the meanings of unfamiliar English words while checking the result against context. Recognize that roots provide clues, not complete definitions.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: The root 'bio' relates to life, so 'biography' concerns a person's life; context confirms the precise meaning.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not assume every word containing similar letters shares the same root or meaning; historical spelling and borrowed forms can mislead.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify useful roots, infer plausible meanings, verify them in context, and distinguish root clues from full dictionary definitions.

subtopics.title: context precision
subtopics.teaching: Choose the vocabulary meaning that fits the exact context, register, grammatical role, and nuance of a sentence. Compare near-synonyms rather than accepting the first broadly related definition.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: 'economical' means avoiding waste or expense, while 'economic' relates more generally to the economy; context determines the correct choice.
subtopics.pitfall: A synonym can be broadly similar but still wrong because of connotation, collocation, register, or part of speech.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: distinguish near-synonyms, use context precisely, explain why alternatives fail, and select vocabulary appropriate to meaning and register.

subtopics.title: collocations
subtopics.teaching: Learn natural word partnerships such as 'make a decision,' 'strong evidence,' and 'deeply concerned.' Collocations are conventional combinations that fluent English tends to prefer.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: Both 'strong evidence' and 'powerful evidence' may be understandable, but 'strong evidence' is the standard collocation in formal English.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not translate word combinations directly from another language or assume any grammatically possible adjective-noun pairing is equally natural.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify common collocations, complete them accurately, detect unnatural combinations, and apply them in original sentences.

subtopics.title: nuance
subtopics.teaching: Distinguish fine differences in meaning, connotation, intensity, and attitude between related words. Use context to determine which shade of meaning the writer intends.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: 'confident,' 'assertive,' 'arrogant,' and 'conceited' all relate to self-assurance but differ substantially in evaluation and intensity.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not treat near-synonyms as interchangeable when the emotional or social implication changes the message.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: compare nuanced vocabulary choices, explain connotations, rank degrees of meaning, and select wording that matches a precise communicative intention.

subtopics.title: academic vocabulary
subtopics.teaching: Interpret and use formal vocabulary common in analytical and educational writing, including terms such as analyze, infer, contrast, evaluate, significant, and consequently.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: 'Evaluate the evidence' asks for a judgment based on criteria and evidence, not simply a summary of what the evidence says.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not substitute everyday words automatically when a question depends on the technical distinction between academic command terms.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: understand academic command vocabulary, distinguish related terms, and apply them accurately when reading or responding.

subtopics.title: complex sentences
subtopics.teaching: Analyze complex sentences by identifying independent and dependent clauses and understanding how subordination expresses relationships such as cause, condition, contrast, and time.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: In 'Although the route was longer, we arrived early because traffic was light,' the clauses express contrast and cause within one sentence.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not mistake sentence length for complexity; a long list can be simple, while a short sentence may contain meaningful subordination.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: parse complex structures, identify clause relationships, preserve meaning when rewriting, and explain punctuation choices.

subtopics.title: clauses
subtopics.teaching: Distinguish independent clauses, which can stand as complete sentences, from dependent clauses introduced by subordinators or relative markers. Identify noun, adjective, and adverb clause functions.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: In 'I know that the team won,' the clause 'that the team won' functions as the object of 'know.'
subtopics.pitfall: A dependent clause may contain a subject and verb but still be incomplete in meaning or grammatical function when separated from the main clause.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify clause boundaries and types, explain their functions, and combine or separate clauses without creating fragments or faulty structures.

subtopics.title: agreement
subtopics.teaching: Apply subject-verb and pronoun-antecedent agreement by identifying the true grammatical subject rather than being distracted by nearby nouns.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: 'The collection of rare books is valuable' takes 'is' because 'collection' is the singular subject, not 'books.'
subtopics.pitfall: Do not match the verb to the closest noun automatically; intervening phrases and compound structures can hide the grammatical subject.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify agreement relationships in complex sentences, correct errors, and explain why the grammatical subject controls the form.

subtopics.title: modifiers
subtopics.teaching: Place modifiers close to the words they logically describe so that meaning is clear and unintended interpretations are avoided. Recognize misplaced and dangling modifiers.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: 'Walking through the museum, Maya noticed the sculpture' clearly makes Maya the person walking; a dangling version would wrongly suggest the sculpture was walking.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not judge a modifier only by whether the sentence sounds familiar; check who or what the modifier logically describes.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify modifier errors, repair ambiguous constructions, and explain how placement changes meaning.

subtopics.title: tense consistency
subtopics.teaching: Maintain logical tense relationships across a passage while allowing deliberate shifts for changes in time, reported speech, or general truths.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: 'She entered the room and noticed that the lights were off' uses past forms consistently for linked past events.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not force every verb into the same tense when the time relationship genuinely changes; consistency means logical alignment, not mechanical uniformity.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify unjustified tense shifts, preserve intended time relationships, and edit paragraphs for coherent tense use.

subtopics.title: error identification
subtopics.teaching: Edit systematically for grammar, usage, word choice, punctuation, agreement, tense, and sentence structure. Read the complete sentence before deciding which segment contains the error.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: In 'Neither of the answers are correct,' identify the singular subject 'neither' and correct the verb to 'is.'
subtopics.pitfall: Do not select an error simply because a phrase sounds unusual; verify it against the grammatical rule and the intended meaning.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: locate errors efficiently, name the underlying rule, distinguish real errors from acceptable variation, and produce a corrected sentence.

subtopics.title: sentence transformation
subtopics.teaching: Transform sentences while preserving their essential meaning, tense, logical relationships, and required grammatical information. Common transformations include active/passive, direct/indirect speech, joining clauses, and changing degree or structure.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: 'People speak English worldwide' can become 'English is spoken worldwide' without changing the core proposition.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not change tense, emphasis, negation, or meaning accidentally while altering the grammatical form.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: perform multiple transformation types accurately, preserve meaning, and explain the grammatical changes made.

subtopics.title: punctuation
subtopics.teaching: Use punctuation to clarify sentence boundaries, relationships, lists, quotations, and emphasis. Understand the functions of commas, semicolons, colons, apostrophes, quotation marks, and dashes.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: A semicolon can join closely related independent clauses when no coordinating conjunction is used; a colon can introduce an explanation or list after a complete clause.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not use commas simply where a reader might pause. Punctuation follows grammatical structure as well as rhythm and style.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: correct punctuation in complex sentences, explain each mark's function, and distinguish grammatical necessity from optional stylistic punctuation.

subtopics.title: style
subtopics.teaching: Analyze style as the combined effect of diction, sentence structure, imagery, formality, rhythm, and rhetorical choices. Style should be described with evidence rather than vague labels.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: Short sentences, direct verbs, and concrete nouns can create a brisk, accessible style, while longer periodic sentences and formal diction can create a reflective or academic style.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not confuse style with tone. Tone is the writer's attitude; style is the characteristic way that attitude and ideas are expressed.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify distinctive stylistic features, connect them to textual effects, compare styles across passages, and support judgments with precise evidence.

subtopics.title: passage editing
subtopics.teaching: Edit a complete passage by checking meaning, grammar, cohesion, word choice, punctuation, and consistency together. Read beyond individual sentences so that corrections improve the passage as a whole.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: When editing a paragraph, first locate the main idea and sentence relationships, then correct agreement and punctuation, remove repetition, and replace vague wording without changing the intended message.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not correct every unusual expression automatically; some variation is intentional. An edit is valid when it improves correctness or clarity while preserving meaning and context.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: edit multi-sentence passages accurately, prioritize errors, preserve the writer's intended meaning, and explain the rule or clarity improvement behind each major correction.

subtopics.title: theme
subtopics.teaching: Identify a text's theme as a central idea about life, society, values, or experience rather than a one-word topic. Track recurring events, conflicts, images, and outcomes to infer the theme.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: A story in which a proud character learns to accept help after repeated failures may develop the theme that humility can enable growth.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not confuse theme with plot or topic. 'Friendship' is a topic; a statement such as 'trust is strengthened by honest communication' expresses a theme.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: distinguish topic from theme, trace supporting details, compare themes across texts, and formulate a precise thematic statement.

subtopics.title: characterization
subtopics.teaching: Analyze characterization through direct description and indirect evidence from actions, dialogue, thoughts, relationships, and reactions. Consider how a character changes or remains consistent.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: A character who quietly returns a lost wallet despite needing money is characterized through action as honest and principled.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not infer a permanent trait from one isolated action without considering context and repeated evidence.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: infer character traits from textual evidence, explain motivations, trace development, and distinguish explicit description from supported inference.

subtopics.title: imagery
subtopics.teaching: Analyze imagery as language that creates sensory or conceptual impressions. Identify the senses or associations involved and explain how imagery contributes to mood, setting, theme, or meaning.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: Describing rain as 'silver threads against the dark roofs' creates visual imagery that can make an ordinary scene feel delicate or reflective.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not label every descriptive adjective as imagery; explain the sensory or figurative effect and its role in the passage.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify significant imagery, explain its effect, connect images to larger meanings, and compare imagery across texts.

subtopics.title: poetic devices
subtopics.teaching: Recognize and interpret devices such as metaphor, simile, personification, alliteration, repetition, contrast, rhyme, and symbolism. Focus on the effect of the device, not just its name.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: Repetition of a key phrase at the beginning of successive lines can emphasize an idea and create rhythm or insistence.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not identify a device without explaining why the poet uses it; a correct label alone does not establish interpretation.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify relevant devices accurately, explain their effects, and integrate device analysis into a coherent interpretation.

subtopics.title: comparative interpretation
subtopics.teaching: Compare two texts by establishing a meaningful criterion such as theme, character, imagery, viewpoint, or treatment of an idea. Support similarities and differences with evidence from both texts.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: Two poems may both present nature as powerful, but one may emphasize comfort while the other presents nature as unpredictable and threatening.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not write two separate summaries and call them comparison. Each paragraph should establish a relationship between the texts.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: construct balanced comparisons, select evidence from both texts, explain significance, and reach a nuanced comparative conclusion.

subtopics.title: argument
subtopics.teaching: Construct an argument with a clear claim, logically ordered reasons, relevant evidence, explanation, and an appropriate conclusion. Anticipate reasonable counterarguments when the task requires persuasion.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: To argue for a school reading program, state the claim, present evidence about reading benefits, explain how the evidence supports the claim, address a practical objection, and conclude with a specific recommendation.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not substitute strong language for reasoning. A persuasive paragraph needs a defensible claim and evidence connected by explanation.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: develop a coherent evidence-based argument, organize reasoning, address counterclaims, and maintain an appropriate formal or persuasive register.

subtopics.title: narrative
subtopics.teaching: Build a narrative around purposeful characters, setting, conflict, sequence, and resolution. Use viewpoint, pacing, dialogue, and sensory detail to make events meaningful rather than merely listing them.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: A story about a lost key becomes engaging when the search reveals a character's fear of disappointing a parent and the resolution changes that relationship.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not overload a narrative with events that do not affect the conflict. Each major event should contribute to tension, character, or resolution.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: sustain a coherent plot, develop character and setting, control pacing and viewpoint, and produce a satisfying resolution.

subtopics.title: descriptive
subtopics.teaching: Create vivid description by selecting precise nouns, verbs, sensory details, comparisons, and spatial organization. Description should guide the reader's attention and create a deliberate impression.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: Instead of saying a market was 'busy,' describe overlapping voices, bright fabric stalls, warm spice smells, and narrow paths between shoppers.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not pile up adjectives without purpose. Precise verbs and selected sensory details usually create stronger description than long lists of modifiers.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: create a consistent descriptive effect, select purposeful sensory details, organize space clearly, and vary sentence structure for impact.

subtopics.title: summary
subtopics.teaching: Condense a source by selecting its central ideas and essential supporting points while preserving the original meaning. Use concise paraphrase rather than copying sentences or adding personal opinions.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: A long passage about water conservation can be reduced to its main problem, two key causes, and the author's proposed solution if those elements drive the passage.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not include every example or minor detail, and do not introduce information that the source does not contain.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify central ideas, prioritize information, paraphrase accurately, maintain objectivity, and produce a concise coherent summary.

subtopics.title: structured response
subtopics.teaching: Organize a response so that each paragraph has a clear purpose, evidence or explanation, and a link to the question. Use introductions and conclusions proportionately rather than padding the answer.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: A literature response can state an interpretation, analyze two quotations or details, explain their significance, and conclude by returning to the central interpretation.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not treat structure as a set of empty headings. Organization is effective only when ideas progress logically and each piece of evidence is explained.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: plan and produce coherent multi-paragraph responses, maintain focus, integrate evidence, and adapt structure to the task.

subtopics.title: analogies
subtopics.teaching: Solve verbal analogies by identifying the precise relationship between the first pair and applying the same relationship to the second pair. Common relationships include function, degree, category, part-whole, cause-effect, and contrast.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: 'thermometer : temperature :: compass : direction' works because each instrument measures or indicates the second concept.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not choose an option merely because the words are related; the type and direction of the relationship must match.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify relationship types, preserve relationship direction, reject near-matches, and solve unfamiliar analogies with justification.

subtopics.title: logical completion
subtopics.teaching: Complete statements or arguments by preserving their logical constraints, grammatical structure, and contextual meaning. Determine what must follow rather than what could merely follow.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: If every member of a club has an ID and Priya is a member, the logically valid completion is that Priya has an ID.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not add assumptions not given in the question. A plausible real-world statement may still be logically unsupported.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: distinguish necessary from possible conclusions, track premises accurately, and complete verbal logic without importing unstated assumptions.

subtopics.title: word relationships
subtopics.teaching: Analyze semantic relationships such as synonymy, antonymy, category membership, part-whole, function, degree, and cause-effect. The exact relationship matters more than broad association.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: 'puppy : dog' expresses a young-to-adult relationship, while 'wheel : bicycle' is part-to-whole.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not treat any two associated words as equivalent relationship pairs; specify what connects them and preserve direction.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify precise semantic relations, classify pair types, and apply the same relation consistently to new word pairs.

subtopics.title: classification
subtopics.teaching: Classify words or concepts using a clear shared criterion, then identify the item that does not belong or the category that best fits. Test each option against the same rule.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: violin, cello, and flute are instruments, but flute differs from the first two if the criterion is stringed instruments.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not change the classification rule midway to justify an attractive answer. The strongest solution uses one consistent criterion that fits the set.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: infer classification rules, handle overlapping categories, identify exceptions, and explain why each selected item fits or does not fit.

subtopics.title: verbal puzzles
subtopics.teaching: Solve verbal puzzles by translating wording into explicit constraints, organizing information, and testing possibilities systematically. Useful representations include tables, ordering lists, and simple condition sets.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: For a puzzle about four speakers with different presentation times, write the time slots and place each constraint before testing the remaining possibilities.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not rely on intuition when several conditions interact; one missed constraint can make a seemingly reasonable answer invalid.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: extract constraints, choose an efficient representation, eliminate impossible cases, and justify the unique or best-supported solution.

subtopics.title: functional texts
subtopics.teaching: Read practical texts such as forms, schedules, advertisements, emails, menus, announcements, and notices for purpose, audience, key details, conditions, and implied actions.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: A timetable question may require combining departure time, platform information, and a stated transfer condition rather than locating one isolated number.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not assume the most prominent detail is the answer. Check headings, footnotes, conditions, dates, and units of information.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: extract actionable information, integrate multiple details, identify audience and purpose, and answer practical questions precisely.

subtopics.title: instructions
subtopics.teaching: Interpret instructions by identifying sequence, conditions, exceptions, required materials, and the exact action expected at each step. Preserve order when order affects the result.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: In a multi-step experiment, heating before adding a reagent may be essential; reversing the steps can change the outcome.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not skim command words such as 'before,' 'unless,' 'only,' or 'except'; these small terms often determine the correct interpretation.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: follow and paraphrase procedures accurately, detect conditional requirements, identify missing or conflicting steps, and predict outcomes from instructions.

subtopics.title: notices
subtopics.teaching: Read notices for essential information including event, audience, date, time, location, eligibility, restrictions, and required action. Distinguish central instructions from decorative language.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: A competition notice may state that registration closes Friday and that participants must bring identification; both details affect what the reader must do.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not infer eligibility or deadlines from general wording when the notice gives explicit conditions elsewhere.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify all action-critical details, infer the intended audience and purpose, and distinguish mandatory requirements from optional information.

subtopics.title: dialogues
subtopics.teaching: Interpret dialogues by tracking speakers, turn-taking, implied meaning, register, intention, and how each response relates to what came before. Dialogue often communicates indirectly.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: If one speaker says 'The room is rather warm' and the other opens a window, the exchange implies a request even though no direct request was made.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not interpret each line in isolation; tone, relationship, and previous turns can change the meaning of a response.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify speaker intention, infer implied requests or attitudes, track conversational logic, and distinguish literal from pragmatic meaning.

subtopics.title: information synthesis
subtopics.teaching: Synthesize information by combining relevant points from multiple sentences or sources into a single supported conclusion. Remove repetition and distinguish agreement, contrast, and complementary evidence.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: If one paragraph reports increased rainfall and another reports flooding after drainage changes, synthesis should connect the environmental and infrastructure evidence rather than merely list both facts.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not merge claims that conflict without acknowledging the conflict, and do not add conclusions that none of the sources support.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: integrate information accurately, reconcile or flag differences, select the strongest combined evidence, and formulate a concise supported conclusion.

subtopics.title: time management
subtopics.teaching: Allocate competition time according to question difficulty, marks, and uncertainty. Use planned checkpoints, avoid spending disproportionate time on one item, and reserve time for review.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: A candidate can complete high-confidence questions first, mark uncertain items, then return to longer inference or reasoning questions with remaining time.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not turn time management into rushing. Accuracy, deliberate checking, and knowing when to move on are part of efficient performance.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: create a realistic time plan, adjust pacing during a test, prioritize effectively, and use remaining time for targeted review.

subtopics.title: elimination
subtopics.teaching: Eliminate answer choices using textual evidence, grammar, logic, meaning, and contradiction before choosing among the survivors. Elimination is strongest when each rejected option has a specific reason.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: In a reading question, remove an option contradicted by the passage, one that answers a different question, and one that makes an unsupported absolute claim before comparing the remaining choices.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not eliminate an option simply because it sounds unfamiliar; unfamiliar wording can still be correct.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: apply systematic elimination, identify distractor types, justify exclusions, and combine elimination with positive evidence for the final choice.

subtopics.title: evidence selection
subtopics.teaching: Select the smallest set of details that directly supports the answer or interpretation. Prefer precise, relevant evidence over decorative or loosely related quotations.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: To support a claim that a character becomes more confident, choose a later action or statement showing changed behavior rather than a descriptive detail about the setting.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not choose evidence merely because it contains the same vocabulary as the question; relevance and explanatory value matter more than word overlap.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: select strong evidence efficiently, explain its relevance, distinguish primary from weak support, and integrate evidence into a reasoned answer.

subtopics.title: precision checking
subtopics.teaching: Perform a final accuracy check for wording, tense, agreement, punctuation, logical consistency, units of meaning, and whether every answer actually addresses the question asked.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: After selecting an inference answer, reread the passage and verify that the answer is supported without an absolute claim that the text never establishes.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not change a correct answer during review without a concrete reason. Checking should target identifiable errors rather than creating doubt for its own sake.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: detect subtle errors efficiently, verify answer-question alignment, and make evidence-based corrections during review.

subtopics.title: mixed language sets
subtopics.teaching: Handle a mixed set containing reading, vocabulary, grammar, editing, reasoning, and communication items by switching methods deliberately rather than using one strategy for every question.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: A vocabulary item may require contextual meaning, a grammar item a structural check, and a reading item evidence retrieval; classify the task before solving it.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not let the method from one question type carry over automatically to another. Identify the skill being tested first.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: classify question types quickly, select the appropriate solving method, maintain accuracy across switches, and review the weakest category strategically.
